summary: The Shear wave velocity calculator returns shear modulus from the 2 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Shear wave velocity calculator work?
sections.html:
The Shear wave velocity calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports shear modulus in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the material); then you type in the shear wave velocity.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 13 options, such as aluminum, brass and copper. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Shear wave velocity calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Shear modulus=density × (shear wave velocity ^ 2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in megapascals, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilograms per cubic meter, and convertible to any of the 9 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Pressure, opening in megapascals
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Speed, opening in meters per second

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Shear wave velocity calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the shear wave velocity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Shear wave velocity calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 1 drop-down on this page offers a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Shear wave velocity calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns shear modulus, derived from the shear wave velocity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Shear wave velocity calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the shear wave velocity, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter shear modulus in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Shear modulus opens in megapascals and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Shear modulus = 0 MPa. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Shear wave velocity calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
